newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO foreign ministers to meet on Bosnia, enlargement.
newsitem.headline: NATO foreign ministers to meet on Bosnia, enlargement.

text.p: NATO foreign ministers meet in Brussels this week to give final approval to a new peace mission in Bosnia and review internal reforms necessary if the alliance's plans to expand eastwards are to go ahead.

The 16 ministers of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) will also hold another session with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov whose country remains resolutely opposed to NATO's enlargement plans.
Western leaders have made clear time and again that the accession talks of at least some former communist states in eastern and central Europe will start next year whatever Moscow's objections.

Russia found itself isolated again on that issue at a summit in Lisbon last week of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), although NATO countries agreed to update the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty.

Diplomats say NATO foreign ministers will play down the differences with Russia over enlargement, stressing Moscow's decision to remain in the alliance-led force in Bosnia and its desire to open talks on a new Russia-NATO charter.
The idea of a charter, covering all aspects of relations between the two former Cold War foes, has been around a long time, but little progress has been made on giving it substance.

NATO officials say the alliance will urge Primakov to make progress on exchanging military liasion officers between NATO's military and political headquarters and Russia's ministry of defence and top military commands.
"Russia has shown interest in this before, and we hope to make some progress there," said one senior official.

Last week, NATO ambassadors put the finishing touches to a plan to replace an Implementation Force (IFOR) overseeing the Dayton peace accords in Bosnia with a smaller Stabilisation Force (SFOR) for a further 18 months.
"All the 16 allies are thoroughly comfortable with the operation plan, it will now go to ministers for final approval," said one senior alliance diplomat.
Once the SFOR plan is approved, the United Nations Security Council will adopt a resolution giving it full legitimacy and it will take over duties from IFOR on December 20.

Diplomats say it is unlikely the ministers will fix a precise date for a summit of NATO leaders next summer which will formally invite certain countries clamouring to join the alliance to begin formal accession talks.
But other than that, they will do much preparatory work and review the candidacies of some 13 hopefuls.
"This is the curtainraiser, this is the ante-chamber to the great moment," added the diplomat.

The same summit is set to back the internal reform of NATO, designed to make it flexible enough to admit new members and undertake more Bosnia-style peacekeeping missions now its Cold War purpose is at an end.

But the reform process has been held up over a row between the United States and France over who is to command NATO's vital southern flank which the meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday is unlikely to be able to resolve.
Ever since the alliance was set up in 1949, an American officer has held the Naples-based southern command, which carries with it control of the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean.
Now, France is demanding this post be handed over to a European, arguing the issue goes to the heart of a U.S commitment to create a distinct European identity within the U.S.-dominated alliance.
Paris has hinted the issue could delay France's plan to rejoin NATO's military structure, which it left 30 years ago, and in turn delay the entire enlargement process.

The ministers will also review plans to boost the alliance's Partnership for Peace programme so as to offer some support to those countries who want to join the alliance, but will not be in the first wave of new members.

"It is very important we come up with something substantial because many of those who will not be among the new members will be very disappointed," Danish Defence Minister Hans Haekkerup told reporters last week.
Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are the favourites to become the alliance's first new members for more than two decades.
